newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-ITALY'S KOSTNER WINS THE SKAARDAL WAY.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-ITALY'S KOSTNER WINS THE SKAARDAL WAY.

text.p: Isolde Kostner, imitating a Norwegian and emulating a compatriot, retained her super-giant slalom world title to complete Italy's golden hat-trick at the Alpine skiing championships on Tuesday.

The 21-year-old from the German-speaking village of St. Ulrich in Val Gardena overcame a poor start to clock one minute 23.50 seconds down the Kandahar-Banchetta piste and beat Germany's Katja Seizinger by 0.08 seconds.

Seizinger, the Olympic downhill gold medallist and former super-G world champion, was in turn 0.06 ahead of compatriot Hilde Gerg -- the first time since the 1952 Oslo Olympics that two German women have been on an Alpine podium.
It was Italy's third gold in three women's races and the host nation moved to the top of the medals table.

Kostner, who won the super-G last year in the southern Spanish resort of Sierra Nevada, also became the second Italian woman in as many races to retain a world title after Deborah Compagnoni successfully defended her giant title on Sunday.
"I was never troubled by all of the attention," said Kostner, shrugging off the huge expectations in Italy after Compagnoni won the first two women's races.
"Deborah is still the queen of skiing because she has two gold medals here," she added.

While matching Compagnoni's achievement in defending a title, Kostner revealed that Norwegian veteran Atle Skaardal, who retained his men's super-G title in the opening race of the championships, had been more of an inspiration.
"I was inspired by Skaardal's victory and the way he skied the bottom part of the course," she said.
"I tried to follow his line and it was the right thing to do because I won...I knew that I could win on this course as Skaardal has the same skis as me."
Her fans, making the journey from north-eastern Italy to the north-west, had been expecting Kostner to dominate the race after winning the last World Cup super-G in January.
But their spirits must have dimmed as the home favourite lagged at the second intermediate and looked to have an impossible task after the third and final one.
Instead, the eighth starter made up more than 0.40 seconds in the final stages to snatch the victory.
"I thought I'd go well on the upper part and have a few problems at the bottom. In fact it was the other way round," she said. Skaardal's race eight days ago was just the same.
Seizinger, who set off fifth right after Gerg, made a few mistakes that sent her wide of the racing line.
"The eight-hundredths stink," she said of the winning margin. "The result, however, is no surprise."

Gerg, who won a super-G in Val d'Isere in December, said she knew that Seizinger and Kostner always had a good chance of beating her after she crossed the line but it was still a disappointment for it to have been so close.
Both Germans will have a chance to turn the table on the Italian in Saturday's downhill although Kostner also has a very real chance of a second gold in that race.
She has won three World Cup downhills in her career, one in January and all in Italy, to just one super-G.
Before 1996, no Italian woman had ever won a recognised world championship race.
They have now surpassed the men, who have never won three golds at any one championships, and could even come close to the Swiss team of 1987 that won every women's race.
Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg, winner of two World Cup super-Gs this season, finished in seventh place.
She clocked 1:24.47 after losing time coming off the final jump and skiing wide. "I made a big mistake on one of the last turns," the Swede said. "I really blew it."
